summary: Specifies how to make DNS dynamic updates secure, so only authorized parties can add or change records. It uses transaction signatures and keys to authenticate update requests and decide who may change which names. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Imagine a phone book anyone could scribble in. This adds a password-like check so only the right people can change an entry.

questions: how to secure dns dynamic updates
what is tsig in dns update
why does dns update use sig0 instead of dnssec sigs
subtitle: How a DNS server decides who may change a zone: sign the update request, then check the signer against policy.

tldr.problem: DNS dynamic update lets clients insert and delete records in a zone, but without protection anyone could change the zone's contents.
tldr.mechanism: Every secure update message carries a TSIG or SIG(0) signature that identifies the sender (the principal). The zone's primary server then checks that principal against a locally configured policy, which by default allows nothing.
tldr.outcome: Authentication of the update request is kept separate from DNSSEC validation of the data. RFC 3007 obsoletes RFC 2137 and updates RFC 2136 and RFC 2535.

today: RFC 3007 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2137 and updates RFC 2136 and RFC 2535. The metadata for this site lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem and the Approach
sections.content:
RFC 3007 defines a way to secure dynamic updates of the Domain Name System, so that only authorized sources can change a zone's contents. It builds on the existing unsecured update operations rather than replacing them. An update can specify insertions or deletions of data, along with prerequisites, and all tests and changes are restricted to a single zone and performed at the zone's primary server. The primary server must increment the zone's SOA serial number when an update occurs or before the next retrieval of the SOA.

The RFC says it obsoletes RFC 2137, an alternate proposal for secure dynamic update, due to implementation experience. It also updates portions of RFC 2535 (in particular section 3.1.2) and RFC 2136.
sections.eli5: Some people can already add and remove names in the phone book. This document adds a way to prove who you are before the phone book lets you do it.

sections.title: Message Authentication Versus Data Authentication
sections.content:
The RFC compares two kinds of protection. Message authentication with TSIG or SIG(0) protects the whole message with a single signing and single verification. For update requests, the signature can establish the authority to make the request, based on policy or key negotiation.

DNSSEC SIG records protect individual records or record sets with the authority of the zone owner, and the RFC says they cannot sufficiently protect an update request. It gives these reasons:

  • Signing the record sets in an update would be incompatible with how update works and would need multiple expensive public key operations.
  • SIG records do not cover the message header, which includes record counts, so record sets could be maliciously inserted or removed without a verification failure.
  • If SIGs protected the prerequisite section, it would be impossible to tell whether the SIGs were themselves a prerequisite or just there for validation.
  • When a record set is deleted, there is no data for a SIG to cover.

As a result, all zone data modified in a signed zone MUST be signed by a relevant zone key, while host and user keys are used only to authenticate messages. This completely disassociates authentication of an update request from authentication of the data itself.
sections.eli5: Signing the whole letter on the envelope is easier and safer than signing every sentence inside it. The sentences get their own official stamp later, once they are in the book.

sections.title: Who Sent the Update
sections.content:
TSIG or SIG(0) records MUST be included in all secure dynamic update messages, so the server can verifiably determine the originator. That originator is the principal, and how it is found depends on the signature:

  • With a SIG(0), the principal is the owner of the KEY record that generated the signature.
  • With a TSIG from a statically configured shared secret, the principal is the same as or derived from the shared secret name.
  • With a TSIG from a dynamically configured shared secret, the principal is the one that authenticated the TKEY process. If the TKEY process was unauthenticated, that shared secret MUST NOT be used for secure dynamic update.

SIG(0) signatures SHOULD NOT be generated by zone keys, since transactions are initiated by a host or user, not a zone. Ordinary DNSSEC SIG records MAY be in an update message but MUST NOT be used to authenticate it. If an update is signed with an unauthorized key, the server MUST return RCODE REFUSED.
sections.eli5: Before the librarian changes anything, she checks your signed library card. A card you made up on the spot does not count, and she tells you no.

sections.title: Policy: What a Principal May Change
sections.content:
All policy is configured by the zone administrator and enforced by the zone's primary name server. By default a principal MUST NOT be permitted to make any changes to zone data; any permissions MUST be enabled through configuration.

The RFC keeps policy in server configuration, not in the protocol, for three reasons: it avoids limits from squeezing policy into a fixed number of bits such as the KEY record's signatory field, policy matters only to the server applying it, and a policy change should not cause interoperability failures.

Implementations SHOULD let policies use the principal as an authorization token, and SHOULD allow per-name access control, with concise ways to name the principal's own name, its subdomains and all names in the zone. They SHOULD also allow restriction by record type. User types are all types except SOA, NS, SIG and NXT. SOA and NS SHOULD NOT be modified by normal users because they create or modify delegation points. NXT records MUST NOT be created, modified or deleted by dynamic update, which is an update to RFC 2136. Beyond these standard policies, users are free to implement any policy they like.
sections.eli5: Knowing who you are is not enough. The teacher also keeps a list of which lines each student may change, and at the start the list is empty.

sections.title: Interaction with DNSSEC
sections.content:
The protocol does not change how updates to secure zones are processed, but the RFC clarifies several points. An authorized update MAY include SIG records with each record set, though they are not required. If the principal may update SIG records, they are added without verification, and the server MAY drop SIGs whose validity period is in the past. If an update tries to delete SIG records, the server MAY override the authority and refuse, for example by allowing deletion only of SIGs not made by a zone key.

If the zone is secured, the affected record set MUST be signed according to the zone's signing policy once the update completes. That usually needs one or more SIG records from zone keys whose private parts MUST be online. When a record set changes, the server MAY delete all its associated SIG records, since they are no longer valid.

If any change is made, the server MUST, if necessary, generate a new SOA record and new NXT records and sign them with the right zone keys. SOA updates are allowed, since maintaining SOA parameters is outside the scope of the DNS protocol.
sections.eli5: After someone changes a line, the old official stamp on it is no longer true. The librarian puts a fresh stamp on the new line herself.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The design requires a zone key, and possibly other secret material, to be held on an online, network-connected host, most likely a name server. That material is at the mercy of host security. Exposing it puts DNS data at risk of masquerade attacks, both for zones served by the machine and for zones delegated from it.

Allowing updates of KEY records may also lead to undesirable results, because a principal could insert a public key without holding the private key and possibly masquerade as the key owner.
sections.eli5: The stamp has to be kept where the teacher can reach it, and that means a thief could reach it too. And letting a student write a new name card for somebody else is risky.
